Immanuel Kant's second critique, formally titled "Critique of Practical Reason" (Kritik der praktischen Vernunft), published in 1788, is a foundational work in moral philosophy. It complements his first critique, "Critique of Pure Reason," which focuses on theoretical reason, by exploring the nature and scope of practical reason, which is concerned with actions and moral duties.

In this work, Kant aims to establish a rational foundation for morality independent of empirical considerations. He argues that moral actions are determined by the categorical imperative, a universal moral law that applies to all rational beings. The categorical imperative is derived from the concept of duty and is formulated in several ways, including the principle that one should act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.

Kant distinguishes between hypothetical imperatives, which are conditional and based on desires or goals, and the categorical imperative, which is unconditional and based on reason alone. He asserts that the categorical imperative is the only principle that can provide a basis for moral obligation because it is grounded in the autonomy of the will, which is the capacity to act according to one's own rational principles.

The "Critique of Practical Reason" also discusses the concept of the "highest good," which Kant defines as the perfect proportion of virtue and happiness. He argues that the highest good can only be achieved if we assume the existence of God and the immortality of the soul, as these are necessary conditions for the possibility of a world where virtue is rewarded with happiness.

Overall, Kant's second critique is a profound exploration of the nature of moral obligation and the role of reason in guiding human action, setting the stage for much of the subsequent development in moral philosophy.
